UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT

No. 23-2847

MARIA GONZALEZ,
  Plaintiff-Appellant,

v.

CITY OF SPRINGFIELD, a municipal corporation, and OFFICER JAMES TAYLOR, individually and in his official capacity,
  Defendants-Appellees.

Appeal from the United States District Court for the Central District of Illinois.
No. 3:22-cv-00891 — Judge Robert Harrison, presiding.

OPINION

WOOD, Circuit Judge.

Maria Gonzalez appeals the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the City of Springfield and Officer James Taylor on her claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for excessive force in violation of the Fourth Amendment and municipal liability under Monell v. Department of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978).

I. BACKGROUND

On March 15, 2022, Officer Taylor responded to a domestic disturbance call at Gonzalez's residence. Upon arrival, Officer Taylor encountered Gonzalez on her front porch. According to Gonzalez, she was unarmed and compliant with Officer Taylor's instructions. Despite this, Officer Taylor allegedly used a Taser on Gonzalez, causing her to fall and sustain injuries including a fractured wrist and concussion.

Officer Taylor maintains that Gonzalez was aggressive and non-compliant, and that his use of the Taser was a reasonable application of force under the circumstances.

II. STANDARD OF REVIEW

We review the district court's grant of summary judgment de novo, construing all facts and drawing all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party. Scott v. Harris, 550 U.S. 372, 378 (2007). Summary judgment is appropriate when there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a).

III. ANALYSIS

A. Excessive Force Claim

Claims of excessive force during an arrest are analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard. Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386, 395 (1989). The inquiry requires balancing the nature and quality of the intrusion on the individual's Fourth Amendment interests against the countervailing governmental interests at stake. Id. at 396.

The relevant factors include: (1) the severity of the crime at issue; (2) whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to the safety of officers or others; and (3) whether the suspect is actively resisting arrest or attempting to evade arrest by flight. Id.

Here, the parties present fundamentally different accounts of the encounter. Gonzalez maintains she was compliant and non-threatening, while Officer Taylor asserts she was aggressive. At the summary judgment stage, we must credit Gonzalez's version of events. Under her account, the use of a Taser against an unarmed, compliant individual responding to a domestic call would constitute excessive force.

The district court erred by crediting Officer Taylor's version of events over Gonzalez's at the summary judgment stage. We REVERSE the grant of summary judgment on the excessive force claim and REMAND for further proceedings.

B. Qualified Immunity

Officer Taylor asserts qualified immunity. Qualified immunity shields government officials from civil damages liability unless their conduct violates clearly established statutory or constitutional rights. Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223, 231 (2009).

Taking the facts in the light most favorable to Gonzalez, a reasonable officer would have known that using a Taser on an unarmed, compliant individual violated the Fourth Amendment. We therefore deny qualified immunity at this stage.

IV. CONCLUSION

The judgment of the district court is REVERSED in part and REMANDED for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT

No. 23-2847

MARIA GONZALEZ,
Plaintiff-Appellant,

v.

CITY OF SPRINGFIELD, a municipal corporation, and OFFICER JAMES TAYLOR, individually and in his official capacity,
Defendants-Appellees.
Appeal from the United States District Court for the Central District of Illinois.
No. 3:22-cv-00891 — Judge Robert Harrison, presiding.

OPINION

WOOD, Circuit Judge.

Maria Gonzalez appeals the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the City of Springfield and Officer James Taylor on her claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for excessive force in violation of the Fourth Amendment and municipal liability under Monell v. Department of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978).

I. BACKGROUND

On March 15, 2022, Officer Taylor responded to a domestic disturbance call at Gonzalez's residence.
Upon arrival, Officer Taylor encountered Gonzalez on her front porch.
According to Gonzalez, she was unarmed and compliant with Officer Taylor's instructions.
Despite this, Officer Taylor allegedly used a Taser on Gonzalez, causing her to fall and sustain injuries including a fractured wrist and concussion.

Officer Taylor maintains that Gonzalez was aggressive and non-compliant, and that his use of the Taser was a reasonable application of force under the circumstances.

II.

STANDARD OF REVIEW

We review the district court's grant of summary judgment de novo, construing all facts and drawing all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party.
Scott v. Harris, 550 U.S. 372, 378 (2007).
Summary judgment is appropriate when there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
Fed.
R. Civ.

III. ANALYSIS

A. Excessive Force Claim

Claims of excessive force during an arrest are analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard.
Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386, 395 (1989).
The inquiry requires balancing the nature and quality of the intrusion on the individual's Fourth Amendment interests against the countervailing governmental interests at stake.
Id. at 396.

The relevant factors include: (1) the severity of the crime at issue; (2) whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to the safety of officers or others; and (3) whether the suspect is actively resisting arrest or attempting to evade arrest by flight.

Id.

Here, the parties present fundamentally different accounts of the encounter.
Gonzalez maintains she was compliant and non-threatening, while Officer Taylor asserts she was aggressive.
At the summary judgment stage, we must credit Gonzalez's version of events.
Under her account, the use of a Taser against an unarmed, compliant individual responding to a domestic call would constitute excessive force.
The district court erred by crediting Officer Taylor's version of events over Gonzalez's at the summary judgment stage.
We REVERSE the grant of summary judgment on the excessive force claim and REMAND for further proceedings.

B. Qualified Immunity

Officer Taylor asserts qualified immunity.
Qualified immunity shields government officials from civil damages liability unless their conduct violates clearly established statutory or constitutional rights.
Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223, 231 (2009).
Taking the facts in the light most favorable to Gonzalez, a reasonable officer would have known that using a Taser on an unarmed, compliant individual violated the Fourth Amendment.
We therefore deny qualified immunity at this stage.
IV.

CONCLUSION

The judgment of the district court is REVERSED in part and REMANDED for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
